lede: Millions of carbon compounds exist, and you never learn them one at a time. Carbon's four bonds build chains of any length, and the chains fall into families whose members step up by one CH₂. Learn a family's rules and you know its members.
can: Give the four features of a homologous series, and define a hydrocarbon for both marks.
Use CnH2n+2 to write any alkane's formula, and draw a structural formula by counting to four.
Name methane, ethane, propane and butane, with each one's formula and state at room temperature.

md: There are millions of carbon compounds, far too many to learn one by one, and you do not have to. They sort into families, and every member of a family follows the same rules, so the rules of one family cover members you have never met. This topic is the first family: the alkanes.

md: Every carbon atom forms **four covalent bonds**: no more, no fewer. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons, drawn as one line. A carbon can bond to other carbons and still have bonds to spare, so carbon atoms join into chains of any length, with hydrogen on the spare bonds. That is why there are so many carbon compounds, and why sorting them into families makes them manageable.

stem: Hydrogen forms one covalent bond and carbon forms four. Explain why carbon can build chains of any length but hydrogen cannot. [3]

steps.working: A carbon atom has four bonds to make, so it can join to another carbon and still have three bonds left.
steps.decision: Start from the number of bonds: it decides what an atom can join to.

steps.working: A carbon at the end of a chain still has bonds to spare, so another carbon can always be added: the chain can keep growing.
steps.decision: A chain grows only if the atom at its end has a bond to spare.

steps.working: Hydrogen has only one bond. Once it has joined something it has none left, so it can only cap the end of a chain.
steps.decision: Say what the other atom cannot do: hydrogen ends a chain and never extends one.

prompt: A student draws a carbon atom with five lines coming from it. What is wrong with the drawing?
options: carbon forms four bonds, so one line is too many
nothing: carbon can form as many bonds as there is room for
carbon forms two bonds, so three lines are too many
answer: carbon forms four bonds, so one line is too many
explain: Carbon forms exactly four covalent bonds, so a fifth line cannot be there. Counting the lines at every carbon, as step 1 of See it counts the bonds a carbon has to make, is how you check any structure you draw.

optionNotes.option: nothing: carbon can form as many bonds as there is room for
optionNotes.why: Carbon's number of bonds is fixed at four; room on the page makes no difference to it.

optionNotes.option: carbon forms two bonds, so three lines are too many
optionNotes.why: Two bonds belongs to oxygen. Carbon forms four, so only one line is extra here.

twin.prompt: Another drawing shows a carbon atom with only three lines coming from it. What is wrong?
options: one bond is missing: carbon needs four
nothing: three bonds is enough for a carbon
one line is too many: carbon forms two bonds
twin.answer: one bond is missing: carbon needs four
twin.explain: Carbon needs four bonds, so a carbon with three lines has one missing. Step 1 of See it starts from this: a carbon always has four bonds to make.

optionNotes.option: nothing: three bonds is enough for a carbon
optionNotes.why: Three is one short. Every carbon in a structure you draw must show four lines.

optionNotes.option: one line is too many: carbon forms two bonds
optionNotes.why: Carbon forms four bonds, not two, so the drawing needs one more line, not one fewer.

title: Why some carbon compounds are no family
md: Methane, ethanol and ethene all contain carbon, but they are not one homologous series: they have three different general formulae and react in different ways. A family needs all four features at once. You need the alkanes' names only up to butane; the longer ones below are here for their numbers.

stem: The table gives four alkanes after butane. Use it to show that they belong to one homologous series. [4]

steps.working: Every formula fits one general formula, CnH2n+2: pentane has 5 carbons and 2 × 5 + 2 hydrogens, and the same holds on every row.
steps.decision: Test the general formula on every row, not just one.

steps.working: Each formula is one carbon and two hydrogens more than the one before it: they differ by CH₂.
steps.decision: Compare neighbours: the step between them is the feature.

steps.working: The boiling points rise steadily, 36, 69, 98 and 126 °C: a gradation in a physical property.
steps.decision: Read the trend from the data and name it with the specification's word, gradation.

steps.working: All four have only C–C and C–H single bonds, so they react in the same kinds of way: similar chemical properties.
steps.decision: Chemical properties come from the bonds, and the bonds are the same kind in every member.

title: GCSE Chemistry - Hydrocarbons - Alkanes & Homologous Series
why: A second run through the family, the general formula and the names, beside our own worked steps.

prompt: Two alkanes differ by C₂H₄. Could they be next to each other in the series?
options: no: neighbours differ by one CH₂ only
yes: any difference in carbon and hydrogen will do
yes: C₂H₄ is the step between neighbours
answer: no: neighbours differ by one CH₂ only
explain: No. Neighbours differ by exactly one CH₂, as step 2 of See it found row by row. C₂H₄ is two CH₂ steps, so another member sits between them.

optionNotes.option: yes: any difference in carbon and hydrogen will do
optionNotes.why: The step is fixed at one carbon and two hydrogens. A bigger gap means a member is missing in between.

optionNotes.option: yes: C₂H₄ is the step between neighbours
optionNotes.why: C₂H₄ is two CH₂ groups together, so it spans two steps, not one.

twin.prompt: Which pair could be next to each other in the alkanes?
twin.explain: C₁₄H₃₀ is one carbon and two hydrogens more than C₁₃H₂₈: one CH₂, the step that step 2 of See it found between neighbours.

optionNotes.why: That gap is C₂H₄, two CH₂ steps, so one member is missing between them.
Same number of carbons with two fewer hydrogens is not the CH₂ step, and C₁₃H₂₆ does not fit CnH2n+2.

md: A **hydrocarbon** is a compound (or molecule) that consists of **hydrogen and carbon only**. Without the word *only*, the sentence also fits ethanol, which has oxygen as well. Every alkane is a hydrocarbon, but not every hydrocarbon is an alkane: an alkene such as propene is a hydrocarbon too.

title: The definition earns two marks
md: One mark for **carbon and hydrogen atoms**, one for **only**. Call them atoms: the 2025 reports record marks lost where they were called ions or molecules.

stem: Which of these are hydrocarbons: C₇H₁₆, C₂H₅OH, CCl₄ and C₃H₆? Give a reason for each. [4]

steps.working: C₇H₁₆ has carbon and hydrogen and nothing else: a hydrocarbon, and an alkane.
steps.decision: Read the elements from the formula, then ask whether anything besides C and H is there.

steps.working: C₂H₅OH also has oxygen, in the OH: not a hydrocarbon.
steps.decision: One extra element rules a compound out: that is the word only at work.

steps.working: CCl₄ has carbon and chlorine but no hydrogen: not a hydrocarbon.
steps.decision: Both elements must be there; carbon with anything else does not count.

steps.working: C₃H₆ has carbon and hydrogen only: a hydrocarbon, but not an alkane, because 2 × 3 + 2 is 8, not 6.
steps.decision: Hydrocarbon is about which elements; alkane is about the formula as well.

prompt: Which of these is a hydrocarbon?
explain: C₅H₁₀ contains carbon and hydrogen only, so it is a hydrocarbon, even though it is not an alkane (step 4 of See it). CH₃OH has oxygen too, and CO₂ has no hydrogen.

optionNotes.why: It has carbon and hydrogen, but the O is oxygen as well, so it is not hydrogen and carbon only.
It has carbon but no hydrogen at all, and a hydrocarbon needs both elements.

twin.prompt: Which of these is NOT a hydrocarbon?
twin.explain: C₂H₅Cl has chlorine as well as carbon and hydrogen, so it fails the word only, as step 2 of See it showed for oxygen.

optionNotes.why: C₈H₁₈ is carbon and hydrogen only, so it is a hydrocarbon; it is an alkane too.
C₄H₈ is carbon and hydrogen only, so it is a hydrocarbon, even though it is not an alkane.

text: 4. The alkanes and their general formula

md: The **alkanes** are the hydrocarbons with the general formula $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$: for **n** carbon atoms there are **2n + 2** hydrogen atoms. They are **saturated**: every bond is a single bond. To use the formula, **double the carbons, then add two**, and write the finished formula with one number after each element. A formula left as a sum earns nothing.

stem:
(a) Give the molecular formula of the alkane with 15 carbon atoms. [1]
(b) An alkane has 78 hydrogen atoms. How many carbon atoms does it have? [1]

steps.working: (a) Hydrogens = 2 × 15 + 2 = 32.
steps.decision: Double the carbons first, then add the two end hydrogens.

steps.working: (a) The formula is C₁₅H₃₂, with the sum finished.
steps.decision: One number after each element: C₁₅H₃₀₊₂ is a rule, not a formula.

steps.working: (b) Work backwards: take off 2, then halve. (78 − 2) ÷ 2 = 38 carbons.
steps.decision: Undo the steps in reverse order: the 2 went on last, so it comes off first.

steps.working: (b) Check forwards: 2 × 38 + 2 = 78, so the alkane is C₃₈H₇₈.
steps.decision: A backwards answer is only safe once you have run it forwards.

prompt: An alkane has 17 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it have?
explain: 2 × 17 + 2 = 36: double the carbons, then add two, as step 1 of See it did for 15 carbons. The alkane is C₁₇H₃₆.

twin.prompt: An alkane has 19 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it have?
twin.explain: 2 × 19 + 2 = 40, the same two moves as step 1 of See it: C₁₉H₄₀.

md: The first four alkanes are named by their number of carbons: **meth** 1, **eth** 2, **prop** 3, **but** 4, and every name ends **-ane**. A **molecular formula** counts the atoms. A **structural formula** (a displayed formula) shows **every atom and every bond** as a line.

To draw one, draw the carbon chain first, then add hydrogens until every carbon has four lines. An end carbon is joined to one carbon, so it carries three hydrogens; a carbon inside the chain is joined to two, so it carries two.

steps.working: Draw five C atoms in a row, joined by four single bonds.
steps.decision: Chain first. An alkane is saturated, so every carbon-to-carbon bond is single.

steps.working: The two end carbons have used one bond each: three H on each. The three inside carbons have used two: two H on each.
steps.decision: Count to four at every carbon; the spare bonds are where the hydrogens go.

steps.working: That is 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 hydrogens, which matches 2 × 5 + 2: the formula is C₅H₁₂.
steps.decision: Two routes to one count: add up the drawing, then check it with the general formula.

prompt: A chain of six carbon atoms is drawn with only its carbon-to-carbon bonds. How many hydrogen atoms go on each end carbon?
explain: Three. An end carbon is joined to one carbon, so three of its four bonds are spare, as step 2 of See it found for pentane.

twin.prompt: In the same six-carbon chain, how many hydrogen atoms go on each carbon inside the chain?
twin.explain: Two. An inside carbon is joined to two carbons, which leaves two of its four bonds for hydrogen, as in step 2 of See it.

text: 6. Why boiling points rise, and states

md: Along the family the molecules get bigger, and bigger molecules attract each other more strongly. More energy is needed to pull them apart, so the **boiling point rises** with each CH₂: that is the gradation.

For a **state at room temperature (20 °C)**, compare 20 °C with the melting and boiling points. Below the melting point it is a solid; between the two, a liquid; above the boiling point, a gas. Methane, ethane, propane and butane all boil below 20 °C, so all four are **gases**.

stem: Pentane melts at −130 °C and boils at 36 °C. What is its state at 20 °C? Explain your answer. [2]

steps.working: 20 °C is above pentane's melting point, −130 °C, so it has already melted.
steps.decision: Compare with the melting point first: above it, the solid has gone.

steps.working: 20 °C is below its boiling point, 36 °C, so it has not boiled: pentane is a liquid.
steps.decision: Between the melting and boiling points means liquid. Name the state and give the comparison: that is the mark.

prompt: An alkane with 20 carbon atoms melts at 37 °C and boils at 343 °C. What is its state at 20 °C?
explain: Solid: 20 °C is below its melting point, 37 °C, so it has not melted. Make the melting-point comparison first, as step 1 of See it did.

optionNotes.why: A liquid needs 20 °C above the melting point, and 37 °C is higher than room temperature.
It boils at 343 °C, far above room temperature, so it cannot be a gas at 20 °C.

twin.prompt: Heptane melts at −91 °C and boils at 98 °C. What is its state at 20 °C?
twin.explain: Liquid: 20 °C is above −91 °C and below 98 °C, so heptane has melted but not boiled, the two comparisons of steps 1 and 2 of See it.

optionNotes.why: A gas needs 20 °C to be above the boiling point, and 98 °C is far above room temperature.
A solid needs 20 °C to be below the melting point, but −91 °C is far below it.

md:
Five ways a right idea loses its mark:
**1.** Name the **family** from its formula: CnH2n+2 alkanes, CnH2n alkenes, CnH2n+1OH alcohols. Not one member, such as ethene.
**2.** Write a **finished formula**: work out 2n + 2 and put one number after the H, never a sum.
**3.** A structural formula shows **every bond**: each H needs its own line.

**4.** In the hydrocarbon definition, carbon and hydrogen are **atoms**, not ions or molecules.
**5.** Chemical properties are **similar**, not the same and not different, and the step between members is **CH₂**, not CH₃.

title: What the reports record
md: The Summer 2025 C2 reports record the CnH2n family named as the alkanes or as ethene, the twelve-carbon alkane left with its arithmetic unfinished, and the hydrocarbon definition losing *only* or calling the atoms molecules or ions. In 2023 few saw that four small alkanes were all gases.

stem:
Mark two answers.
(a) "A hydrocarbon is a compound made of carbon and hydrogen ions only." [2]
(b) The formula of the alkane with 23 carbon atoms, written as C₂₃H₄₆₊₂. [1]

steps.working: (a) The word only is there: that mark is earned.
steps.decision: Mark each point on its own: only, then carbon and hydrogen atoms.

steps.working: (a) Carbon and hydrogen are called ions, but in a hydrocarbon they are atoms, so that mark is lost: 1 out of 2.
steps.decision: The 2025 reports name atoms called ions or molecules as a mark lost.

steps.working: (b) That is a rule with the sum left undone: 0 out of 1. The finished formula is C₂₃H₄₈.
steps.decision: A formula carries one number after each element; do the sum, then write it.

prompt: Mark this definition of a hydrocarbon out of 2: 'a molecule that contains carbon and hydrogen'.
explain: 1 mark: carbon and hydrogen are named, but the word only is missing, so ethanol would fit too. Step 1 of See it marks the word only on its own.

optionNotes.why: Without the word only, the sentence also fits ethanol, which has oxygen, so the only mark is not earned.
Carbon and hydrogen are both named, which earns one mark even without the word only.

twin.prompt: Mark this one out of 2: 'a compound consisting of only carbon and hydrogen atoms'.
twin.explain: 2 marks: the word only and the carbon and hydrogen atoms are both there, the two points that steps 1 and 2 of See it look for.

optionNotes.why: Nothing is missing: only is there, and carbon and hydrogen are called atoms.
Both marking points are present, so this earns full marks.

prompt: An alkane has 21 carbon atoms. A student writes its formula as C₂₁H₄₂₊₂. How many hydrogen atoms should the finished formula show?
explain: 44: double 21 to get 42, then add the 2, as step 3 of See it finished its formula. One number after each element: C₂₁H₄₄.

twin.prompt: An alkane has 31 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does its finished formula show?
twin.explain: 64: 2 × 31 + 2. Finish the sum, as in step 3 of See it, and write C₃₁H₆₄.

md: The general formula is not a fact to take on trust: it follows from carbon's four bonds. Count the bond ends in a straight chain of n carbons. Whatever is not used joining the carbons to each other must hold a hydrogen.

stem: Show that an alkane with n carbon atoms has 2n + 2 hydrogen atoms. [4]

steps.working: Each carbon has four bonds, so n carbons have 4n bond ends between them.
steps.decision: Count what is available before counting what is used.

steps.working: A straight chain of n carbons has n − 1 carbon-to-carbon bonds, and each uses two bond ends, one from each carbon: 2(n − 1) ends.
steps.decision: Joining things in a line always takes one link fewer than the number of things.

steps.working: The ends left over each hold one hydrogen: 4n − 2(n − 1) = 4n − 2n + 2 = 2n + 2.
steps.decision: Subtract the ends used from the ends available, then open the bracket with care.

steps.working: So the formula is CnH2n+2. For one carbon it gives 2 × 1 + 2 = 4 hydrogens: methane, as it should.
steps.decision: Test a proof on the smallest case you already know.

prompt: Use the same counting for a straight chain of 40 carbon atoms. How many carbon-to-carbon bonds join them?
explain: 39: one bond fewer than the number of carbons, as step 2 of See it said, because 40 atoms in a line need 39 links.

twin.prompt: For that chain of 40 carbons, how many bond ends are left for hydrogen?
twin.explain: 4 × 40 = 160 ends, minus 2 × 39 = 78 used: 82 left, the subtraction of step 3 of See it. That is 2 × 40 + 2.

md: The general formula also gives the relative formula mass of any alkane. Each carbon brings 12 and each of its 2n + 2 hydrogens brings 1, so Mr = 12n + 2n + 2 = 14n + 2. Run it backwards and a relative formula mass tells you which alkane you have.

stem: An alkane has a relative formula mass of 86. Find its molecular formula. [3]

steps.decision: Write the general Mr as an equation with the value you are given.

steps.working: Take off 2, then divide by 14: n = (86 − 2) ÷ 14 = 6.
steps.decision: Undo the operations in reverse order.

steps.working: 6 carbons and 2 × 6 + 2 hydrogens: C₆H₁₄. Check: 6 × 12 + 14 × 1 = 86.
steps.decision: Always check by working the Mr forwards from your formula.

prompt: An alkane has a relative formula mass of 114. How many carbon atoms does it have?
explain: 8: take off 2 and divide by 14, as step 2 of See it did. (114 − 2) ÷ 14 = 8, so the alkane is C₈H₁₈.

twin.prompt: Another alkane has a relative formula mass of 212. How many carbon atoms does it have?
twin.explain: 15: (212 − 2) ÷ 14, the reverse steps of step 2 of See it. The alkane is C₁₅H₃₂.
